question_text: Provide a detailed timestamped narration of this surgical procedure.
reference_narration:
[00:18 - 00:22] paracentesis creation: A keratome is used to create a paracentesis incision in the peripheral clear cornea of the right eye, which has a very shallow anterior chamber and a dense white cataract.
[00:22 - 00:27] anterior capsule staining: Trypan blue dye is injected through the paracentesis into the shallow anterior chamber to stain the anterior capsule, improving its visibility for the capsulorhexis.
[00:27 - 00:48] viscoelastic injection: A cohesive viscoelastic is injected to deepen the very shallow anterior chamber and create space. Following this, a clear corneal main incision is created with a keratome.
[00:48 - 01:21] capsulorhexis: A cystotome is used to puncture the anterior capsule of the intumescent lens, releasing some liquefied cortex. Capsulorhexis forceps are then used to carefully tear and complete a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC).
[01:21 - 01:50] hydrodissection: A cannula is placed under the anterior capsule flap, and balanced salt solution (BSS) is injected to separate the lens nucleus from the surrounding cortex and capsule.
[01:50 - 02:20] phacoemulsification: A phaco probe and a chopper are introduced into the anterior chamber. The dense white nucleus is emulsified and aspirated from within the capsular bag using a chopping technique.
[02:20 - 02:50] cortical irrigation and aspiration (i/a): An irrigation/aspiration (I/A) handpiece is used to remove the remaining cortical material from the capsular bag, leaving it clean for IOL implantation.
[02:51 - 03:22] hydrodissection: The video switches to the left eye. Trypan blue dye is injected, followed by viscoelastic to deepen the chamber. A cystotome punctures the intumescent lens capsule, resulting in a gush of milky white liquefied cortex, which is aspirated.
[03:22 - 04:00] capsulorhexis: Using capsulorhexis forceps, the surgeon completes the continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis on the left eye after decompressing the lens.
[04:00 - 04:10] hydrodissection: Balanced salt solution is injected under the anterior capsule to hydrodissect the nucleus in the left eye.
[04:10 - 04:52] phacoemulsification: The phaco probe and chopper are used to disassemble and emulsify the dense white nucleus of the left eye within the capsular bag.
[04:52 - 05:30] cortical irrigation and aspiration (i/a): The irrigation/aspiration handpiece is used to meticulously remove the remaining lens cortex from the capsular bag of the left eye.
[05:30 - 05:40] iol insertion: After filling the capsular bag with viscoelastic, a foldable intraocular lens (IOL) is inserted into the bag using an injector system.
[05:40 - 06:11] iol positioning and viscoelastic removal: A manipulator is used to position the IOL correctly within the capsular bag. The irrigation/aspiration handpiece is then used to remove all the viscoelastic from the anterior chamber.
[06:13 - 06:54] IOL Insertion and Positioning (Right Eye): The video switches back to the right eye. Viscoelastic is removed. An IOL is then inserted into the capsular bag with an injector. Two instruments are used to center and secure the lens haptics within the bag.

question_text: Provide a detailed timestamped narration of this surgical procedure.
reference_narration:
[00:10 - 00:13] paracentesis creation: A sharp blade is used to create a paracentesis incision in the peripheral clear cornea.
[00:13 - 00:23] anterior capsule staining: A cannula is inserted through the sideport incision. VisionBlue dye is injected under the pre-existing viscoelastic to stain the anterior capsule of the mature white cataract.
[00:23 - 00:30] viscoelastic injection: A viscoelastic cannula is used to inject a high-molecular-weight viscoelastic substance (OVD) into the anterior chamber, deepening it and pressurizing the eye.
[00:35 - 00:43] main corneal incision: A keratome blade is used to create the main multi-planar clear corneal incision.
[00:43 - 00:52] phacoemulsification: A bent-needle cystotome is used to puncture the center of the stained anterior capsule. Immediately upon puncture, a large plume of white, milky liquefied cortical material flows out from the capsular bag into the anterior chamber.
[00:52 - 01:12] cortical irrigation and aspiration (i/a): A 27-gauge cannula attached to a syringe is inserted through the capsular opening to aspirate the free-floating liquefied cortex from within the capsular bag, attempting to decompress the intumescent lens.
[01:12 - 01:28] capsulorhexis: A viscoelastic cannula is used to re-inflate the anterior chamber. As the cannula moves, it reveals two large, radial, linear tears extending from the central puncture to the periphery of the anterior capsule. This creates a pattern resembling the Argentinian flag, with two blue-stained capsule flaps separated by the white cataract.
[01:28 - 01:44] capsulorhexis: Micro-scissors are introduced into the anterior chamber. The surgeon carefully cuts the edges of the torn anterior capsule flaps, connecting the radial tears to create a continuous, albeit irregular, capsular opening, converting the complication into a functional can-opener capsulotomy.
[01:44 - 02:13] phacoemulsification: A phaco probe and a chopper instrument are used to perform phacoemulsification. The lens nucleus is grooved, cracked into four quadrants, and each quadrant is then emulsified and aspirated from within the capsular bag.
[02:15 - 02:27] intraocular lens (iol) implantation: An IOL injector cartridge is inserted through the main corneal incision. A single-piece acrylic IOL is injected into the capsular bag, where it unfolds. The trailing haptic is then gently positioned inside the bag.
[02:27 - 02:36] viscoelastic removal (i/a): An irrigation/aspiration (I/A) handpiece is inserted to remove the remaining viscoelastic from the anterior chamber and from behind the newly implanted IOL, ensuring the lens is secure in the capsular bag.
[02:36 - 02:43] wound hydration: A cannula is used to inject balanced salt solution (BSS) into the stroma surrounding the main and sideport incisions, causing localized swelling to create a self-sealing wound.
